cluster_name: Nepal-Tibet glacial flash flood kills 750, over 3,000 missing
event_summary: On 26 August 2026, a glacier collapsed near the Nepal-Tibet border in the Himalayas, triggering catastrophic flash floods and mudslides that killed over 750 people across Nepal and China's Tibet region, left more than 3,000 missing, and stranded hundreds of workers in hydropower tunnels while new barrier lakes raised fears of secondary flooding.
tldr: Headlines across all 24 media markets are locked onto a near-uniform death-toll register — '750 dead, 3,000 missing' — with minimal editorial differentiation between wire services, South Asian, Southeast Asian, and African outlets, implying strong headline compression relative to what the body pass captures. A widely shared rescue-capacity frame foregrounds logistical failures — mud-clogged rivers, new barrier lakes, trapped hydropower workers — most visibly in Turkish, Indian, UK, Kenyan, and wire outlets, and represents the main secondary headline layer separating those markets beyond the casualty count. A distinctly national-diaspora layer in South Korean, Canadian, Nordic, Russian, and Italian outlets personalises the catastrophe through missing citizens, generating headlines more differentiated from each other than the death-toll formula and likely the source of measurable headline-body divergence in those markets. The starkest editorial divide is between Indian, UK, and Taiwan/HK outlets — which headline China's censorship of Tibet flood footage as a major story — and Chinese state outlets, which cover the same event exclusively through a relief-and-aid success narrative with no acknowledgment of information restrictions.

single_outlet_findings.finding: Only headline in the corpus to invoke a climate-justice frame: 'The Floods Nepal Didn't Cause' explicitly names Nepal's non-responsibility for the warming that triggered the glacial collapse ��� a FAIRNESS angle absent from every news outlet, including The Conversation's two climate-science headlines.

Only headline in the corpus to frame the disaster as a warning-system failure rather than a climate threat or death-toll story — 'struck without warning' foregrounds institutional infrastructure failure and implicitly asks whether better early-warning systems would have saved lives, a POLICY_PRESCRIPTION angle invisible in all peer US headlines.

Only headline globally to foreground a local-hero narrative — a teacher's alarm calls saved over 1,600 lives — making individual human agency the lead story while every peer UK outlet led with rescue logistics or China's censorship.

Only headline in the corpus to cast China as a proactive diplomatic aid provider ('China offers aid package for Nepal, says Chinese FM'), presenting a solidarity frame diametrically opposed to the Indian, UK, and SCMP POLITICAL frame of China withholding information about the Tibet-side disaster.

bottom_line: At the headline layer this disaster reads as a mass-casualty emergency with strained rescue infrastructure; the sharpest editorial divide runs between Indian, UK, and Taiwan/HK outlets headlining China's censorship of Tibet flood footage and Chinese state media presenting the same event as a relief success and diplomatic solidarity story.
